case_study_insert.main_stem: Orchard Vale Dairy (OVD) is a cooperative in the dairy processing sector, employing a workforce of 40. Founded in 2016 by the cheesemaker Gwenllian Price, it matures farmhouse cheese for specialist shops and uses a flat structure with democratic leadership and member involvement. OVD plans to invest $480,000 in a cheese maturation cellar, financed by a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $135,000 a year, a variable cost of $5.50 a unit and a selling price of $10.00, and currently produces 50,000 units a year. OVD faces milk waste of 4.8% and a maturation skills gap that limits how much cheese it can age for specialist shops.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations and Quality Log — Q3 2025: The cellars matured 11,800 wheels last quarter at a defect rate of 2.2%, down from 3.9% a year ago. Customer complaints fell from 34 to 17 per month and milk waste was 4.8% of intake. Average delivery to shops is 3.6 days. A survey of 410 shoppers found 66% prefer farmhouse cheese and 53% would pay $1.50 more per wheel. A skills review shows 12 of 40 staff need maturation training; college courses cost $540 per employee.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Financial Position of Orchard Vale Dairy as at 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 4.10% to 4.85%, raising borrowing costs on the cooperative's variable-rate loan. (2) The national minimum wage rises by 6.4% from $12.70 to $13.51 per hour from April 2026. (3) Wholesale milk and feed input costs rose 7.9% year-on-year, while farmhouse cheese sales grew 5.2%.

questions.question_text: OVD plans to fund its $480,000 cellar with a $300,000 bank loan and $180,000 retained profit. Explain two advantages for OVD of using retained profit rather than a larger bank loan for the $180,000 portion.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit is internal cash with no interest charge and no repayment timetable, so the rise in the base rate from 4.10% to 4.85% cannot raise the cost of this part of the $480,000 cellar. With fixed costs of $135,000 a year, saving interest protects the $4.50 contribution on each of the 50,000 wheels and gives the cooperative steadier cash flow while it services the $300,000 loan.

Point 2: Retained profit requires no collateral and no bank approval, so Gwenllian Price can spend the $180,000 quickly on the cellar without pledging cooperative assets. A larger bank loan would add debt and could restrict how the cooperative is run; using its own profits keeps decision-making with the members and demonstrates the strength of the business when OVD next seeks finance.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage of retained profit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation applied to OVD, its $480,000 cellar and its financing.

questions.question_text: OVD wants to sell more of its farmhouse cheese. Consider selling through specialist shops, farmers' markets, or an e-commerce website. Which should OVD choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Specialist shops: These already stock OVD's cheese and can display it to the 66% of 410 shoppers who prefer farmhouse cheese, reinforcing the 3.6-day delivery promise. Shops take a margin and may demand reliable supply of the 11,800 wheels matured last quarter, which the 12 untrained staff and 4.8% milk waste could threaten. Shelf space is limited and the shop controls the customer relationship.

Farmers' markets: Direct selling at markets lets OVD keep the full $10.00 price, explain the farmhouse story to shoppers and receive immediate feedback, which suits a cooperative with democratic leadership. It builds a loyal local customer base cheaply. The reach is small, it consumes staff time from a workforce of 40, and sales are weather- and location-dependent, so it cannot absorb the full 50,000-wheel output the $480,000 cellar is meant to hold.

E-commerce website: A website reaches shoppers beyond the local area, showcases the farmhouse image that 66% prefer and captures the 53% who would pay $1.50 more without a shop's margin. It gives OVD direct customer data for repeat sales. Set-up and delivery of a chilled product are costly and complex, and a cooperative of 40 with a 4.8% milk-waste problem may struggle with packing and returns.

Recommendation: OVD should choose the e-commerce website, supported by a few specialist shops. Online sales reach the 66%/53% segments nationally and protect the $4.50 contribution needed for the $480,000 cellar, whereas farmers' markets are too small for 50,000 wheels and specialist shops give away margin and control. The main risk, chilled delivery, can be managed with a limited local radius before expanding.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the channels with minimal application to OVD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of at least two channels in OVD's context with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Discussion of all three channels with a justified recommendation explaining why shops and markets are secondary.

questions.question_text: OVD uses a flat structure with democratic leadership, but 12 of 40 staff need maturation training and milk waste is 4.8%. Explain two benefits for OVD of this leadership style and structure in closing the skills gap.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Democratic leadership lets the 40 members and workers help design the maturation routines, so the 12 needing training are more likely to attend the $540 courses and apply what they learn. In a flat structure their ideas reach Gwenllian Price quickly, speeding changes that cut the 4.8% milk waste and protect the 3.6-day delivery promise to specialist shops.

Point 2: A flat structure gives a wide span of control, so experienced cheesemakers can coach the 12 trainees directly in the cellars instead of waiting for approval through layers. That helps raise the 2.2% defect rate performance and keep 50,000-wheel output on plan. Involvement also raises commitment in a cooperative, reducing resistance to the $480,000 cellar and protecting the $4.50 contribution per wheel.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to OVD's skills gap, waste and output.

questions.question_text: Twelve of OVD's 40 staff need maturation training. Consider on-the-job mentoring in the cellars or external college courses at $540 per employee. Which should OVD choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job mentoring: Experienced cheesemakers can teach the 12 trainees on the actual maturation cellars that the $480,000 investment is building, at no course fee, while the trainees keep working. This protects the 11,800 wheels matured last quarter and suits a cooperative of 40. The limits are that good and bad habits pass on together, certification is limited, and mentors' own work suffers while the 4.8% milk waste still needs attention.

External college courses at $540 per worker: A recognised qualification gives the 12 staff up-to-date maturation science and a certificate, supporting the 66% of 410 shoppers who prefer farmhouse cheese and the 53% who would pay $1.50 more. The cost is 12 × $540 = $6,480, small beside the $480,000 cellar. Staff are away from the cellars temporarily and generic teaching may not match OVD's particular cheeses, so on-site follow-up is still needed.

Decision: OVD should use on-the-job mentoring first, with external college courses for the senior mentors who then train the rest. Mentoring is specific to OVD's cellars, costs no fees and avoids losing output from a workforce of 40 already stretched by the 4.8% waste; the full $6,480 college route is rejected because it removes trainees from production and a certificate alone does not improve the 2.2% defect rate. Once the cellar stabilises, the remaining staff can take the $540 courses.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training options with limited application to OVD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of benefits and drawbacks of both options in OVD's context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both options with a justified decision covering cost, disruption and relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how the management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $135,000 ÷ ($10.00 − $5.50) = $135,000 ÷ $4.50 = 30,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 30,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $10.00 − $5.50 = $4.50. Answer: contribution per unit is $4.50.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways OVD's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Compare the 30,000-unit break-even output with 50,000 wheels produced: the margin of safety is 20,000 wheels, showing how far sales can fall before the $135,000 fixed costs are uncovered.
2. Use the $4.50 contribution to test the $1.50 premium that 53% of shoppers would pay; adding it to the $10.00 price lifts contribution to $6.00, which managers can weigh against the 66% who prefer farmhouse cheese.
3. Use unit cost of $8.20 ($135,000 ÷ 50,000 = $2.70 plus $5.50 variable cost) to monitor the 4.8% milk waste and target the 2.2% defect rate.
4. Use labour productivity of 1,250 wheels per worker (50,000 ÷ 40) to judge whether the 12 trainees can be trained without disrupting the 3.6-day delivery promise from the new cellar.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 30,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $4.50 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 20,000-wheel margin of safety; $1.50 premium pricing; unit cost $8.20 to cut 4.8% waste; labour productivity 1,250 wheels per worker for training plans.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula and method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii); 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate OVD's financial position by calculating the current ratio and the acid test ratio for 2024 and 2025. Has OVD's financial position improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Current Ratio 2024 = 1.63 : 1
Current Ratio 2025 = 1.47 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2024 = 0.88 : 1
Acid Test Ratio 2025 = 0.63 : 1

Detailed workings: 2024 current assets = $90,000 inventories + $55,000 trade receivables + $50,000 cash = $195,000; 2025 current assets = $125,000 + $80,000 + $15,000 = $220,000. The 2024 liquidity comparison is $195,000 ÷ $120,000 = 1.63; the 2025 comparison is $220,000 ÷ $150,000 = 1.47. The stock-excluding measure for 2024 is ($195,000 − $90,000) ÷ $120,000 = $105,000 ÷ $120,000 = 0.88; for 2025 it is ($220,000 − $125,000) ÷ $150,000 = $95,000 ÷ $150,000 = 0.63.

Evaluation: Liquidity has deteriorated. Current assets rose from $195,000 to $220,000, but current liabilities grew faster, from $120,000 to $150,000, so the 2024 figure of 1.63 fell to 1.47 in 2025. The stock-excluding measure fell more sharply, from 0.88 to 0.63, because cash collapsed from $50,000 to $15,000 while inventories rose from $90,000 to $125,000 and receivables from $55,000 to $80,000. Cheese maturing in the cellar ties up cash by nature, but a stock-excluding figure below one means OVD cannot cover short-term debts without selling stock or collecting invoices — risky while it repays a $300,000 loan and has spent $480,000 on the cellar. The 4.8% milk waste makes the bigger inventory still harder to turn into cash, and slower-paying shops explain the receivables rise.

Conclusion: OVD's financial position has not improved; it has worsened. Both measures fell (1.63 to 1.47 and 0.88 to 0.63), and the sharp drop in the stock-excluding figure shows the problem is cash, not just stock. OVD should chase the $80,000 of receivables, reduce the 4.8% waste and rebuild cash before taking on more debt.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or simple changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the current ratio and acid test ratio for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of inventories, receivables, cash and liabilities and a justified conclusion on whether financial position improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for OVD of focusing on farmhouse cheese.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: The research shows 66% of 410 shoppers prefer farmhouse cheese and 53% would pay $1.50 more per wheel, so OVD can raise its $10.00 selling price and protect the $4.50 contribution per unit despite a 7.9% rise in milk and feed costs. The farmhouse image also justifies the $480,000 maturation cellar and helps win specialist-shop listings that support 50,000-wheel output.

Disadvantage: Maturing farmhouse cheese ties up cash in inventories for longer, which already shows up as rising stock of $125,000 and low cash of $15,000, and the 4.8% milk waste reduces usable output. A focus on a niche limits volume because only 66% of shoppers prefer it, and if the 12 trainees lack maturation skills the 2.2% defect rate could rise, threatening the 3.6-day delivery promise.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual development linked to OVD's research, costs and cellar.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the rise in the base interest rate to 4.85%, the 6.4% minimum wage increase and the 7.9% rise in milk and feed costs will affect OVD. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (4.10% to 4.85%): If OVD's $300,000 bank loan is variable-rate, the annual interest cost rises by 0.75% of $300,000 = $2,250 a year (0.0075 × $300,000). That is modest beside fixed costs of $135,000 a year, and a fixed-rate loan would face no increase. Higher rates could slow consumer spending, though farmhouse cheese sales grew 5.2%; fixing the rate would cap this risk.

Minimum wage increase (6.4%, to $13.51 an hour): Some of the workforce of 40 is likely hourly-paid, so wage costs rise. The insert gives no hours worked or pay by role, so an annual wage bill cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 50,000 wheels ÷ 40 workers = 1,250 wheels per worker. If the $480,000 cellar raises output per worker the wage rise is affordable; if the 12 untrained staff and 4.8% milk waste hold output back, unit labour cost rises and the $4.50 contribution shrinks.

Milk and feed input costs (7.9%): These feed the $5.50 variable cost per unit, but the insert does not decompose it, so only a labelled bound is defensible: if the whole variable cost rose 7.9%, that is 7.9% × $5.50 = about $0.43 per wheel; across 50,000 wheels that is roughly $21,500 a year (50,000 × $0.43). The 53% of shoppers who would pay $1.50 more and the 66% preferring farmhouse cheese give real pricing room, which is why this change is less damaging than the figures alone suggest.

Conclusion: The 7.9% milk and feed rise will have the greatest impact. It compounds on every one of the 50,000 wheels and directly erodes the $4.50 contribution supporting the $480,000 cellar; the interest rise is a known $2,250 at most, and the wage rise can be offset by productivity gains from the new cellar, helped by the $1.50 premium shoppers accept.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external factors with limited application to OVD.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on OVD's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes with a justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller.
